conversation.content:
Good morning—thank you for making time for this today. I’m [Dr./Ms.] Rivera, a perinatal mental-health clinician. My job is simply to listen and help you feel supported in these early weeks of motherhood.

We’ll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually called the EPDS. It’s a quick, 10-question check-in about how you’ve been feeling in the past seven days. It screens for common mood and anxiety changes that can show up after birth, and it includes one question about self-harm so we can be sure you’re safe.

Everything you share stays confidential within your medical record, and there are no right or wrong answers. We just want an honest snapshot of how you’re coping so we can tailor the best care for you. I’ll read each question conversationally and jot down your answers—no paperwork on your end.

Ready to start? Here’s the first one:

Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

*lets out a small sigh, eyes a bit watery*

I... I can laugh sometimes, I guess. Like when my mom came over and she made a joke about how I used to put diapers on my dolls when I was little. But mostly... it feels really hard. My husband will try to be funny and I just... I can't. I feel too tired and worried all the time. Everything feels so heavy. Even when I do laugh, it doesn't feel real - like I'm just pretending to be okay.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

*shakes head slowly*

No… not really. I mean, I *want* to, but when my husband cracks a joke I just stare at him. It’s like the laughter is stuck behind this big lump of worry and tiredness. The only time I almost laughed was when the dog sneezed and scared himself, but even that felt… distant, like I was watching someone else enjoy the moment.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

*wrings hands in lap*

I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a new show, even just a quiet shower. Now… nothing feels worth looking forward to. My sister offered to watch the baby so I could get a haircut, and I said yes, but I felt blank inside. I’ll probably go, but it feels like one more chore, not something enjoyable.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

*nods, voice cracking*

All the time. Yesterday she wouldn’t latch, and I sat there crying, telling myself I’m a terrible mom, that she deserves someone who knows what she’s doing. When she fusses for no reason I think it must be something I ate, or that I’m not holding her right. My partner says I’m doing great, but I keep replaying every little thing, convinced I’m messing her up already.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

*clasps hands tightly together*

Yes... almost every day. I'll just be sitting there feeding her and suddenly my heart starts racing because I'm sure something is wrong - like what if she stops breathing or what if I'm not producing enough milk. I check on her constantly when she's sleeping, sometimes I wake her up just to make sure she's okay. My mom says it's normal new mom worry but... this feels different. It doesn't go away even when everything seems fine.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

*nods quickly, eyes darting to the stroller beside the chair*

Yes… a few times. It’s like a sudden wave—my chest gets tight, I can’t catch my breath, and I’m sure something awful is about to happen. Once, I was folding her tiny onesies and my heart started racing; I had to sit on the floor and count my breaths. Nothing triggered it. It just… hits, and then I feel shaky and exhausted after.
Things have been getting on top of me

*voice drops, eyes on the floor*

Most days, honestly. It’s like I’m drowning in small tasks—one bottle, one diaper, one load of laundry—and they pile up until I’m frozen. I’ll look at the dishes and just start crying because I can’t figure out where to begin. I keep thinking, “other moms handle this—why can’t I?” I manage, but it feels like I’m barely treading water, and I’m so tired of the constant effort.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

*exhales shakily, pressing fingertips to temples*

Yeah… pretty much every night. I’ll finally get her down, but then my head starts spinning with everything I did wrong that day and everything that could go wrong tomorrow. I lie there staring at the ceiling, checking the monitor every few minutes. Sometimes I drift off around 3 a.m., only to wake up an hour later with my heart pounding for no reason. I’m exhausted but sleep just… won’t come.
I have felt sad or miserable

*eyes well up; voice is small*

Most of the time. I wake up feeling heavy, like there’s a gray cloud hanging over everything. I look at my beautiful baby and feel… nothing but guilt for not being happier. Little tasks feel huge, and I catch myself just staring out the window, tears slipping down without me noticing. I keep waiting for the “new-mom joy” everyone talks about, but mostly I just feel empty and weepy.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

*nods slowly, dabbing at her eyes with a crumpled tissue*

Yes... a few times this week. Yesterday I cried while changing her diaper because she looked up at me and smiled, and instead of feeling happy I just felt this wave of sadness. I couldn't stop. The tears come out of nowhere sometimes - when I'm folding laundry, when I'm trying to eat, even when I'm holding her. I try to hide it because I don't want her to feel my sadness, but... it's hard to control.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

*shakes head quickly*

No—never. I’ve felt overwhelmed and hopeless, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. My baby needs me, and I want to be here for her. I just want to feel better so I can be the mother she deserves.

You shared that the joy of new motherhood feels distant and heavy right now. Laughing, planning a coffee date, even watching a favorite show once brought excitement, yet lately everything feels flat and burdensome. You tear up describing how irrational guilt floods in when your baby won't latch, how you replay small tasks in a loop each night, and how sudden waves of breathless dread arrive without warning. While you love your daughter fiercely and have not contemplated self-harm, you feel stuck under a gray cloud that blocks the light you hoped would return.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>She reports being unable to laugh even when her husband jokes; laughter feels "stuck," matching "Not at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes complete loss of anticipatory pleasure (anhedonia): activities once enjoyed now feel like chores and evoke no positive emotion, matching "Hardly at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports constant self-blame ('all the time') with vivid examples of blaming herself for normal infant behaviors, matching 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-daily, intrusive, irrational worries about the baby's safety that persist despite reassurance, indicating anxiety 'very often</sym>, <sym>Fallback score from text</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most days," unable to start basic tasks, crying at dishes, and feeling frozen—clearly matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports nightly difficulty falling and staying asleep due to intrusive worries, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive sadness, emotional heaviness, emptiness, and frequent crying—clearly aligns with "Yes, most of the time".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes crying multiple times this week triggered by everyday moments, indicating frequent crying episodes matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Score 25 (≥14 plus functional impairment) places you in the high-risk range on the EPDS. You endorse at least two weeks of daily low mood, loss of interest (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), marked anxiety, sleep disruption beyond infant needs, fatigue, feelings of worthlessness, and difficulty coping-core criteria for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> per <med>DSM-5</med>. No self-harm ideation is present. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>midwife</med>, or <med>primary-care provider</med> within the next few days to discuss symptoms and treatment options
2. Ask about same-week referral to a <med>perinatal mental-health specialist</med> for evaluation, <med>CBT</med>, or medication if indicated
3. Share these results with a trusted support person so they can help coordinate appointments and assist with infant care while you focus on recovery
4. Begin gentle daily structure: one small pleasurable activity (music, short walk) and scheduled 20-minute rest when baby sleeps; keep expectations minimal
5. Practice brief <med>breathing exercises</med> (4-7-8 pattern) when panic sensations arise; place baby in safe crib, sit, inhale 4 s, hold 7 s, exhale 8 s, repeat x4
6. Maintain nutrition and hydration: prep simple snacks (nuts, yogurt) at bedside; accept help with meals to stabilise blood sugar and mood
7. Limit evening screen time and monitor use; blue-light filters and calming audio can ease transition back to sleep during night feeds
8. Monitor safety: if thoughts of self-harm develop, call your local emergency number or go to the nearest emergency department immediately
9. Follow up with EPDS re-screen in 2 weeks to track response to interventions
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Post-partum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother (infant present)  
Date: [today]  

1. Endorsed Symptoms  
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness, anhedonia (Q2, Q8, Q9)  
- Loss of capacity for pleasure/enjoyment, including toward infant (Q1, Q2, Q9)  
- Excessive or inappropriate guilt, self-blame regarding parenting competence (Q3)  
- Clinically significant anxiety: near-daily worry, catastrophic concerns about infant safety, physical symptoms of panic (Q4, Q5)  
- Subjective feeling of “drowning,” being overwhelmed by routine tasks (Q6)  
- Sleep disturbance clearly linked to ruminative worry rather than infant care demands (Q7)  

2. Observations  
- Affect: tearful, constricted; psychomotor slowing noted  
- Cognition: intact; no psychosis  
- Safety: denies suicidal or self-harm ideation (Q10)  
- Insight: good; patient recognizes distress is beyond “normal” new-mom experience  

3. Pattern Summary  
Consistent with moderate-severe postpartum depressive episode with comorbid anxiety. Multiple DSM-5 specifier-level criteria endorsed; functional impairment explicitly described (household tasks “frozen,” social withdrawal, persistent tearfulness).  

4. Risk Factors Flagged  
- Severe guilt / self-criticism  
- Daily panic-equivalent episodes  
- Chronic insomnia secondary to mood  
- Absence of protective pleasure/mastery experiences  
- No self-harm intent currently; continue routine safety monitoring  

5. Screening Impression  
High clinical likelihood of postpartum depression with anxious features; recommend expedited referral for comprehensive psychiatric evaluation and evidence-based treatment (psychotherapy ± medication). Continue safety plan and support-system activation.
